body.heading: Change, measured in years
paragraphs: Evolution — change in the inherited traits of a population over generations — is usually too slow to watch. But when the environment changes suddenly and selection is strong, it can move within a human lifetime, and scientists have measured it happening.

The ingredients are simple: variation within a population, traits that pass to offspring, and some individuals surviving to breed more than others. Given those, the population's average traits shift — no plan or direction required.

body.heading: Moths and finches
paragraphs: In nineteenth-century England, the peppered moth was mostly pale and speckled, matching lichen-covered bark. As factory soot blackened the trees, a dark form — previously rare — was better camouflaged from birds and became common. When clean-air laws let the bark pale again, the pale form returned.

On the Galápagos, researchers Peter and Rosemary Grant measured Darwin's finches for decades. After a severe drought in 1977, only birds with deeper beaks could crack the surviving hard seeds — and the next generation's beaks were measurably deeper. Evolution, recorded with calipers.

body.heading: The fastest evolution on Earth
paragraphs: Bacteria evolve fastest of all, because their generations last minutes and their populations are astronomical. Antibiotics impose brutal selection: the few bacteria with resistance genes survive, multiply, and within years a drug that once worked can fail.

That is evolution with consequences for everyone, and it follows the same rules as the moths and finches — variation, inheritance and selection. Watching it happen has turned evolution from a historical inference into a measurable, ongoing process. The same watching brief now runs in real time in hospitals and on farms, where resistance to drugs and pesticides is tracked season by season, almost like weather.

takeaway: When conditions change fast, evolution can be measured within years: moth colour, finch beaks and bacterial drug resistance have all shifted in living memory.
